ovl.kicker: the oldest light in the universe

ovl.right: A NAME FROM ITS BIGGEST CRITIC
THE OLDEST LIGHT IS ALL AROUND US
IT GREW 10²⁶ TIMES IN A FLASH

num.unit: million years after the Big Bang

ovl.sub: each with its own Big Bang

ovl.kicker: our universe, one bubble of many

caps.text: In New Jersey, America, two scientists were cleaning pigeon droppings out of a giant radio antenna
Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson
Their antenna picked up a strange hiss that would not go away
Day or night, wherever the antenna pointed, the sound stayed the same
They thought the pigeons and their nests were to blame
The pigeons were removed. The antenna was scrubbed clean
The hiss was still there
The hiss was not a fault. It was the oldest light in the universe...
...the echo of the Big Bang
That echo proved the universe had a beginning
Today we know that beginning was 13.8 billion years ago
And according to scientists, in its very first instant, it grew 10²⁶ times bigger
The discovery later won a Nobel Prize
But it also left humanity with its biggest question
What was there before the universe began?
The universe has a birthday, and scientists know it precisely
In 2009, the European Space Agency launched a satellite: Planck
For four years it mapped the whole sky in the same light the New Jersey antenna had caught
Faint patterns hidden in that light tell the age of the universe
In 2018 came Planck's final result: 13.8 billion years
Give or take just 20 million years
When Earth formed, about 4.6 billion years ago...
...the universe was already 9 billion years old
But the first to say the universe had a beginning was not a telescope. It was a priest
Belgium's Father Georges Lemaître was a Catholic priest, and also a physicist
In 1927, he used Einstein's equations to show that the universe is not standing still
It is expanding
That same year in Brussels, Einstein told Lemaître...
"Your calculations are correct, but your physics is abominable"
Two years later, in 1929, America's Edwin Hubble saw distant galaxies racing away from us
And the farther they are, the faster they go
In 1931, Lemaître took the next step
If everything is expanding today, then once, everything must have been together in one place
He called it the primeval atom: the cosmic egg
The idea needed a name...
...and the name came from its biggest critic
28 MARCH 1949
On BBC radio, British astronomer Fred Hoyle was speaking
Hoyle believed the universe had no beginning and no end...
...that it has always been the same
Explaining Lemaître's theory, he used a word...
"BIG BANG"
Hoyle never accepted the theory
But the name he gave it stuck forever
Today every child knows the start of the universe by the name its critic gave it
And Hoyle was proved wrong by the same hiss that is still all around us
After the Big Bang, the universe was so hot and dense that light could not move a single step
About 380,000 years later, it cooled enough for light to break free for the first time
That same light has been travelling for 13.8 billion years
On the way it was stretched so much that it is no longer visible light
Now it is microwaves...
...at just minus 270 degrees Celsius
In 1978, Penzias and Wilson won the Nobel Prize for this discovery
And about 1 percent of the black-and-white static on old TVs, with no channel tuned...
...was this very light
The echo of the Big Bang, on the TV at home
But this light hid a puzzle...
...one that troubled scientists for years
The universe looks the same in every direction
Its far-apart regions never touched each other, yet they are exactly alike
That was the puzzle
7 DECEMBER 1979
On that night, a young American physicist, Alan Guth, wrote in his notebook...
"Spectacular realization"
His idea: in a tiny fraction of the first second, space itself expanded faster than light
10²⁶ times
The whole universe we can see today was then smaller than a proton...
...and in less than the blink of an eye, it grew to the size of a large orange
The expansion got a name: inflation
INFLATION
Inflation explained how the universe expanded
But as soon as scientists turn the clock back further, all of science breaks down
Physics has two great theories
Einstein's gravity explains big things, like galaxies and black holes
Quantum physics explains the smallest things, atoms and particles even smaller
Usually each works fine in its own place
But in the first moment after the Big Bang, everything was both tiny and enormously heavy
There, the two theories clash
Here there is a wall
Cut one second into so many pieces that it takes a 1 followed by 43 zeros...
...the very first slice of time after the Big Bang
PLANCK TIME
No equation can yet say what lies beyond that wall
But scientists have not stopped trying to reach it
17 MARCH 2014
On 17 March 2014, the BICEP2 team in Antarctica announced it had found direct traces of inflation
Scientists around the world celebrated
But months later it turned out the signal had been made by dust in our own galaxy
Then came the James Webb Space Telescope
In 2025, Webb saw the most distant galaxy yet, its light leaving just 280 million years after the Big Bang
The closer Webb gets to the beginning, the clearer it becomes...
...that telescopes alone can't get past the wall
New ideas are needed now...
...and the most startling idea came from Stephen Hawking
Maybe there was nothing before the Big Bang...
...not even time
In 1983, Stephen Hawking and James Hartle proposed an idea
Near the beginning, time does not run the way we know it
Time becomes just like length and width
So the beginning of the universe has no edge at all
Like a ball, it simply rounds off and closes
In 2018, a few weeks before he died, Hawking explained it with an example
Asking what came before the Big Bang is like asking what lies south of the South Pole
There is nothing there, because the South Pole itself is the end point
If Hawking was right, the word "before" has no meaning
But not every scientist agrees with Hawking
Some say there was a whole universe before the Big Bang
In this idea, there was another universe before ours
It shrank and shrank, then bounced back like a ball...
BIG BOUNCE
Nobel Prize-winning British scientist Roger Penrose goes even further
In his view, the universe runs in endless cycles, one after another
In 2018, Penrose's team claimed traces of the previous universe in the echo of the Big Bang
Most scientists don't accept the claim; they say it's just noise
But if Penrose is right, the Big Bang was not the start of the story, just a new chapter
And one idea goes further still...
...that our Big Bang was not alone
Inflation has a strange consequence
Some scientists think the rapid expansion never stopped everywhere at once
Where it stopped, a bubble formed: a universe. Elsewhere, expansion carried on
Just like bubbles rising here and there in boiling water
The idea is called eternal inflation
ETERNAL INFLATION
It keeps making countless bubbles, one after another
Every bubble, a separate universe, each with its own Big Bang
Our universe may be just one bubble...
...a tiny part of a multiverse
Scientists have searched that ancient light for marks of collisions with other bubbles
So far, no firm sign has been found
The wait for an answer may not be long
Japan's LiteBIRD satellite is being prepared to launch around 2032
Its job: to find the real traces of inflation in that echo
It may finally tell how the beginning happened
Until then, the question stays open
Was Hawking right, or Penrose?
Did time really have a beginning, is the universe an endless cycle...
...or is our universe just one of countless bubbles?
Science has not decided yet
In 1964, Penzias and Wilson thought that hiss was a fault...
...today it is the biggest clue to the biggest puzzle of all
Where the universe came from, and what came before it...
...the answer still hides behind that oldest light
